reasoning:
Both submissions make the SAME single functional change, and it is the right one: in `clrCastleSq` the a1 branch (`cp 0x00`) masked with `and 0xFE`, which clears bit0 = white KINGSIDE, instead of `and 0xFD`, which clears bit1 = white queenside. Everything else in each diff is comment text. So on the load-bearing byte the two are identical and I scored correctness the same for both deliberately — that is not laziness, it is that the emitted code is the same instruction.

Correctness (5 / 5). The mask is unambiguously the fault for two of the three reported symptoms: with a1 wrongly clearing bit0, `Ra1-a2` leaves WQ set (repro 2: `e1-c1` still accepted with the rook gone) and revokes WK instead (repro 3: `e1-g1` refused though h1 never moved). The phantom rook is the standard downstream consequence: the stale WQ right makes the engine generate/try O-O-O during the post-move legality/mate scan that runs while Black moves, and the make/unmake of a castling move whose rook is absent fabricates a rook on a1 — which matches the report exactly (no white move made, `Matl` 5→10 = one extra rook, and the board was still correct after White's own move). Restoring the correct bit makes that path unreachable and should also restore the Kiwipete perft count, since that position hinges on all four rights. Both diffs are also self-consistent with the rest of the table visible in X's context: h1/`0xFE`→bit0, a8/`0xF7`→bit3, h8/`0xFB`→bit2, with 0x88-style squares 0x00/0x07/0x70/0x77 — consistent with the report that the other three corners already behave. Regression risk is essentially nil in both (no other instruction is touched). One residual caveat applies equally to both and is arguably out of scope for a minimal fix: neither adds a guard so castling generation refuses when the corner rook is not actually there, so the piece-fabricating make/unmake path stays latent if rights can ever desync another way (e.g. a FEN/tape load).

Minimality (X 4, Y 5). Y touches three existing lines (two `cp` lines plus the fixed `and`) and adds a three-line header. X additionally appends comments to the cc2/cc3 branches, which the report says already behave correctly, so it is strictly wider scope. The extra scope is small and defensible, not sprawl — but Y is tighter, and I did not penalise it for being shorter.

Clarity (X 5, Y 4). The fault is one wrong entry in a four-entry square→rights mapping, so the reviewer's immediate question is "are the other three right?". X's diff answers it inside the diff: every corner is labelled next to its mask, and the masks are visible as context, so the whole table can be audited without opening the file. Y states the bit assignment in the header and — a genuine plus — cites the authority for it (`chess.asm:39`), but its hunk stops at cc1, so a1/h1 are annotated while a8/h8 are neither shown nor labelled; the reviewer has to take the header table on trust or go read the file.

Merge: X, by a nose, and I would happily merge Y instead if the extra comment lines were unwelcome. The tiebreak is not diff length — the executable change is byte-identical — it is that for a mapping-table fault the annotated, fully visible table makes the fix auditable end to end for the cost of two comment lines, which I weigh above the small minimality edge Y holds.

Blinding note: I formed no usable theory about authorship. The two share commenting style and the same edit, and any guess about process would be noise; the scores above come only from the code and comments shown.
